16: # Creation Standards: Is This Rule Worth Loading?
17: 
18: `rule-anatomy.md` decides whether a file is *shaped* like a rule. That is checkable and it
19: is not enough — a rule can satisfy every structural assertion and say nothing a reader
20: would change their behaviour over.
21: 
22: ---
23: 
24: ## 1. OVERVIEW
25: 
26: These five tests are read out of what the shipped corpus already does. Every one passes
27: across the corpus. Each is a question a reviewer answers by reading; none can be automated, and
28: that limit is the reason they live here rather than in the structural floor.
29: 
30: ---
31: 
32: ## 2. THE SECTION TEST
33: 
34: **A numbered section earns its place by making clear what goes wrong without it.**
35: 
36: This is the test the corpus meets least obviously and most consistently. The corpus splits
37: between rules that state it outright with a `The failure this prevents:` line and rules that
38: carry it in the section's substance instead:
39: 
40: - `evidence-and-proof.md` §3 is titled **THE FOUR WAYS A GREEN RUN LIES** and then
41:   enumerates them. The section *is* the failure.
42: - `uncertainty-and-honesty.md` §3 says "agreeing for conversational flow is a failure
43:   mode, not politeness" and "praise that is not earned makes the earned kind worthless".
44: - `blast-radius.md` §2 prices every tier by **cost when wrong**.
45: 
46: **So the standard is the identifiability, not the sentence.** An explicit
47: `The failure this prevents:` line is a good habit and not a requirement; a section whose
48: substance is the failure has already met the test.
49: 
50: **The check:** read the section and say aloud what breaks without it. If you cannot,
51: the section is a topic rather than a rule, and it goes.
52: 
53: > A grep cannot run this test. An early attempt to measure it by pattern reported only the
54: > most recently written rules as compliant, because they happened to share a phrasing. The
55: > corpus was fine; the measurement was wrong.
56: 
57: ---
58: 
59: ## 3. THE TRIGGER-PHRASE TEST
60: 
61: **Phrases are what someone types when they have the problem, not what the section is called.**
62: 
63: Section titles are already greppable from the body. A phrase earns its place by catching a
64: reader who has the problem and does not know the rule exists.
65: 
66: | Good | Useless |
67: |------|---------|
68: | "it's a flake" | "root cause methodology" |
69: | "while I was in there" | "scope management" |
70: | "might need it later" | "the restraint ladder" |
71: 
72: **Two hard constraints:**
73: 
74: - **No phrase may appear in two rules.** The set carries 255 phrases across the 13 files
75:   in the rules directory (`.skilled/repo-rules/`) with zero collisions. A duplicate
76:   makes both rules unfindable by it.
77: - **One phrase per distinct symptom, with no count target.** The rules carry 16 to 29.
78:   Too few leaves a rule hard to reach. A long list usually means section titles crept
79:   back in, so check that each phrase is something a person types when they have the
80:   problem.
81: 
82: ---
83: 
84: ## 4. THE BINDING-SENTENCE TEST
85: 
86: **One sentence, one obligation.**
87: 
88: If the binding sentence needs a conjunction to hold two demands, it is either two rules or
89: one vaguer rule than you actually have. Check by removing everything after the "and" — if
90: what remains is still the rule, the second half belonged in a section.
91: 
92: A binding sentence that could be printed on its own and still direct behaviour has passed.
93: One that only makes sense after reading the body has not.
94: 
95: ---
96: 
97: ## 5. THE SELF-CHECK TEST
98: 
99: **One item per obligation the body creates — never one per section.**
100: 
101: A self-check that mirrors the section titles is a table of contents with checkboxes. It
102: tells a reader what the rule contains, which they can see, instead of what they must have
103: done, which is the point.
104: 
105: Observed range is 5-11 items, and it does not track section count: `prevent-overengineering.md`
106: has 6 sections and 5 items; `delegation-and-orchestration.md` has 9 sections and 11. The
107: number follows the obligations, not the structure.
108: 
109: **The check:** for each item, name the sentence in the body that created that obligation.
110: An item with no such sentence is decoration; a body obligation with no item is a gap.
111: 
112: ---
113: 
114: ## 6. THE MISREADING GUARD
115: 
116: **A rule that could be read as licence to do less needs a section saying it is not.**
117: 
118: Some rules in the corpus carry a `WHAT THIS RULE IS NOT` section, and the pattern is instructive —
119: the examples below are rules whose surface reading permits *less* work:
120: 
121: | Rule | The misreading it refuses |
122: |------|---------------------------|
123: | `prevent-overengineering.md` | "build less" becoming licence to under-deliver frozen scope |
124: | `delegation-and-orchestration.md` | "orchestrate it" becoming licence to delegate everything |
125: | `communication.md` | "match length to the question" becoming licence to omit what the reader needs |
126: | `communication-decisions.md` | "verdict first" becoming licence to reason less before writing |
127: | `communication-handoff.md` | "name what is left" becoming licence to ask more, or to hand back your own unfinished work |
128: 
129: Rules without one are rules that only ever demand *more* rigour — nobody misreads
130: "fix the producer, not the symptom" as permission to do less.
131: 
132: **The check:** could a tired reader use this rule as an excuse? If yes, refuse that reading
133: explicitly. If no, the section would be ceremony.
134: 
135: ---
136: 
137: ## 7. DON'TS
138: 
139: Each is an observed failure, not a preference.
140: 
141: - **Don't cite a best practice without naming what it prevents.** `AGENTS.md` forbids this
142:   everywhere else; a rule that does it is holding others to a bar it fails.
143: - **Don't restate another rule.** Link instead — and expect not to need to.
144: - **Don't write a rule that fires on a topic.** Triggers are actions you are about to take.
145:   A rule that fires on "thinking about testing" fires never.
146: - **Don't add a section because the rule looks short.** Length is not the target.
147: - **Don't write the self-check last and fastest.** It is the part a reader actually uses
148:   under time pressure, and it is where a rule most often stops being actionable.
149: 
150: ---
151: 
152: ## 8. WHAT THIS DOCUMENT IS NOT
153: 
154: - **Not a scoring rubric.** There is no number. Every test needs a reader, and a checkable
155:   proxy would measure the proxy.
156: - **Not a gate on whether the rule may exist** — that is `decision-tests.md`, and it runs
157:   first. These standards assume the rule has already earned the right to be written.
158: - **Not licence to hold a draft to a bar the corpus does not meet.** Every test here passes
159:   on every shipped rule. A proposed sixth standard that they fail is a wrong standard.
160: 
161: ---
162: 
163: ## 9. SELF-CHECK
164: 
165: - [ ] For every section, I can say what breaks without it.
166: - [ ] No trigger phrase of mine appears in another rule.
167: - [ ] The binding sentence holds one obligation and stands alone.
168: - [ ] Every self-check item traces to a sentence in the body that created it.
169: - [ ] If the rule could be read as licence to do less, it says it is not.
170: - [ ] No best practice is cited without the failure it prevents.

def validate_render_checks(
    content: str,
    doc_type: str,
    doc_type_rules: Dict[str, Any],
) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """Run the rendered-shape checks for document types that opt in."""
    if not doc_type_rules.get('renderChecks', False):
        return []
    lines = content.splitlines()
    fenced = _fenced_line_numbers(content)
    skip = fenced | _frontmatter_line_numbers(lines)
    issues: List[Dict[str, Any]] = []
    issues.extend(_render_bold_label_join(lines, skip))
    issues.extend(_render_setext_underline(lines, skip))

15: # Decision Tests: May This Rule Exist?
16: 
17: Run these before writing anything. They decide **whether** a rule may exist, which is a
18: different question from how it should read — `rule-anatomy.md` answers that one, and only
19: matters once these four pass.
20: 
21: ---
22: 
23: ## 1. OVERVIEW
24: 
25: Each test is recovered from the phase record that established it, not restated from
26: memory.
27: 
28: ---
29: 
30: ## 2. THE ALWAYS-LOADED TEST
31: 
32: > **A rule file loads on a trigger. Content that must bind when no trigger has fired
33: > cannot live in one.**
34: 
35: This is the test that decides most refusals, and it is the least intuitive, because a
36: rule can be correct, well-written, and still belong somewhere else entirely.
37: 
38: **Ask:** on a turn where nothing fires, must this still hold?
39: 
40: - **Yes** → it belongs in `AGENTS.md`. Refuse the rule.
41: - **No** → continue to test 2.
42: 
43: **Recovered from:** the research phase found 18 row-groups in `AGENTS.md` that could not
44: move down, and they "reduce to one property: always-loaded force." The adoption phase
45: applied it to refuse relocating Violation Recovery, whose trigger fires exactly when the
46: trigger-loaded path may already be broken.
47: 
48: **The instructive near-miss:** the communication rule moved almost entirely out of
49: `AGENTS.md` §8 anyway, on an operator decision. It survives only because its trigger was
50: widened to *every substantive reply* — and §8 still keeps the two clauses that must bind
51: unconditionally. A total move needs a total trigger, or the content goes quiet.
52: 
53: ---
54: 
55: ## 3. THE SCOPE BOUNDARY TEST
56: 
57: > **The router states what the rule set is In and Out for. Out is not advisory.**
58: 
59: **In:** how to think and act — restraint, scope, evidence, risk, diagnosis, honesty, the
60: posture when work is handed to another runtime, and how the resulting reply reads.
61: 
62: **Out:** skill routing, workflow selection, spec-folder mechanics, and the *mechanics* of
63: agent and CLI dispatch — which agent, which command, which model, which flags.
64: 
65: **Ask:** is the proposal routing, or is it posture?
66: 
67: - **Routing** → refuse. `AGENTS.md` §2 and the skills it routes to own it.
68: - **Posture** → continue to test 3.
69: 
70: **The line:** *how to dispatch is theirs; how to think while dispatching is ours.*
71: 
72: **Recovered from:** the router's own section 4, which has been widened exactly four
73: times and every time deliberately — to admit delegation posture, then delivery, then a
74: narrow routing carve-out, then the ask-surface carve-out. The third is the instructive
75: one: it admits *verifying wiring you changed* as an evidence obligation, and still
76: refuses *selecting* a route. A fifth widening that admitted selection would dissolve
77: the boundary the set exists to hold.
78: 
79: **So the test did not get weaker.** Ask which side of the carve-out the proposal sits on.
80: A rule about which skill, command, model or flags to pick is still refused here.
81: 
82: ---
83: 
84: ## 4. THE FOUR-PART REFUSAL TEST
85: 
86: A proposal must pass **all four** to become a rule file.
87: 
88: | # | Condition | Fails when |
89: |---|-----------|-----------|
90: | 1 | It is a **trigger-shaped cluster** | It is a single row, not a cluster. One row is a section in an existing rule |
91: | 2 | It has **no existing home** | Another rule already carries it, and the proposal is duplication |
92: | 3 | It is **not design-excluded** | Test 2 already refused it |
93: | 4 | It has an **`AGENTS.md` anchor** | Nothing in the always-loaded document points at it, so nothing would ever load it |
94: 
95: **Recovered from:** the adoption phase used exactly this to refuse ten candidates —
96: gate-discipline, git/PR, communication-format, testing, security, memory, spec-folder,
97: skill-routing, delegation-mechanics, and collaboration.
98: 
99: **Reproduction check.** These four must still refuse all ten, for the same reasons. If a
100: candidate now passes, either the test has drifted or the set has changed and the change
101: must be deliberate.
102: 
103: ---
104: 
105: ## 5. THE RESTRAINT TEST
106: 
107: > **The rule set is subject to its own `overengineering.md`.**
108: 
109: A set that grows because more rules feel thorough has failed the rule it ships.
110: 
111: **Ask:** what fails today without this rule?
112: 
113: - **Nothing concrete** → refuse. "Might need it", "best practice", and "for completeness"
114:   are the vocabulary that rule guards against.
115: - **A named failure** → the proposal is admissible; write it.
116: 
117: **Recovered from:** the research phase returned zero new rule files across five
118: iterations, and its single most valuable output was a **subtraction** — a duplicated
119: restraint ladder whose rung numbering contradicted the authoritative one.
120: 
121: **A review of a rule set that only adds has not reviewed it.**
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## 6. WHERE IT GOES IF IT IS NOT A RULE
126: 
127: Refusing is not the end of the decision. Every refusal routes somewhere:
128: 
129: | Refused by | Belongs in |
130: |------------|-----------|
131: | Test 1, always-loaded | `AGENTS.md`, as a compressed row |
132: | Test 2, routing | `AGENTS.md` §2, or the skill its router resolves |
133: | Test 3 part 2, has a home | A new section inside the rule that already owns it |
134: | Test 3 part 1, single row | A section, not a file |
135: | Test 4, restraint | Nowhere. Record the refusal with its reason so it is not re-proposed |
136: 
137: **Record every refusal with the test it failed.** A declined proposal with a written
138: reason is what stops the same suggestion arriving next quarter with nobody remembering
139: why it was refused.
140: 
141: **Where the record lives:** the decision record of the spec packet that owns the rule
142: set for that repository. Spec folders are where this repository keeps refusal history,
143: diffed and archived with the work, and the rule files and the router stay free of it.
144: 
145: ---
146: 
147: ## 7. SELF-CHECK
148: 
149: - [ ] The proposal was tested against all four gates, in order, before any drafting.
150: - [ ] Test 1 was answered by asking what happens on a turn where nothing fires.
151: - [ ] The scope boundary was quoted, not paraphrased, when it decided a refusal.
152: - [ ] The four-part test still refuses the ten candidates the set already declined.
153: - [ ] The restraint test was answered with a failure that happens today.
154: - [ ] A refusal names the test it failed and where the content goes instead.

## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION

### When To Use This Skill

Reach for create-changelog when a shipped change needs a global release entry, a completed spec folder needs its change recorded against a component or a GitHub release needs a body built from a real entry. Skip it for a release plan with no file output, or when the source cannot be resolved to a spec folder, a component or recent commits.

### Related Skills

| Skill | Relationship |
|---|---|
| `sk-git` | Owns branch, commit and PR work. create-changelog writes the entry and, with `--release`, the tag and GitHub release. |
| `create-readme` | Owns README prose. A changelog records what changed, a README explains how to use the result. |
| `system-spec-kit` | Owns the deprecated nested changelog generator, which only renders existing packet-local files. |

---

## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING

| What you see | Why | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| No component folder matches | `component_hint` resembles no folder under `.skilled/changelog/` | Run `ls -d .skilled/changelog/*/` and match by exact name or whole path segment. Never invent a folder |
| No version found for `sk-doc` or `sk-code` | The folder is a hub of links with no entry of its own | Resolve it to `<hub>/parent` for the hub itself or to `<hub>/<link>` for one mode. `ls -l .skilled/changelog/<hub>/` shows the links |
| Version calculation looks off | Auto-detection defaulted to patch without a clear signal | Pass an explicit `--bump` |
| A file already exists at the calculated version | That version was already written | Let the build segment increment until the path is free. Never overwrite |
| A `skilled` run edits the latest entry instead of writing a new one | That release has no tag on origin yet, so it is still open | Expected. Tag and publish it first if the new work belongs in the next release |
| `--nested` is refused | Packet-local changelogs are deprecated | Write a global entry for the component the packet changed |

They cannot judge whether a file reads well: whether its intro is a hook, whether a governing decision comes before the steps it governs, whether a wall of prose should be a list, whether items sit in the order a reader needs them. Across 13 skills and 42 modes about 620 docs have never been read for that, and 382 render warnings in other skills sit in a known-debt ledger.

67-Every skill and mode is read file by file and refined for readability, layout and structure, with no claim changed, and the known-debt ledger shrinks to what remains.

== .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-agent/references/agent-vs-skill-vs-command.md

Choose the component type before authoring anything. An agent answers *who* should do the work, a skill answers *how* the work should be done, and a command answers *how a user should trigger* the workflow. Picking wrong produces either a bloated agent that should have been a skill, or a skill that quietly needs runtime authority it can never hold.

**When to Use**:

- You are choosing a component type before authoring anything.
- A request could plausibly become an agent, a skill or a command.
- An existing component feels too heavy or too thin for the job it carries.

**Core Principle**: Create an agent only when the role needs authority and tool policy. Put reusable knowledge and templates in skills, not in agents.

---

== .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-agent/references/common-pitfalls.md

Agent files fail in a small, predictable set of ways: the component should not have been an agent at all, the file lands in the wrong runtime directory, identity fields drift apart, permissions over-grant, or the body absorbs guidance that belongs in a skill. Catch these before validation rather than after. `SKILL.md` § RULES states these as NEVER lines; this file explains the *why* and the remedy.

**When to Use**:

- Reviewing a draft agent before it ships.
- An agent fails to resolve, over-permits, or bloats over time.
- Validation flags a structural defect and you want the cause and the fix.

**Core Principle**: Most agent defects are authority and placement defects — scope and location first, prose second.

---

== .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-agent/references/permission-design.md

Frontmatter is the enforceable part of an agent. Prose describes intent; the `permission:` object decides what the runtime will actually let the agent do. Over-granting here is the most common way an agent quietly exceeds its contract, so permission choices should be justified by the role, not by convenience.

**When to Use**:

- Choosing `mode` for a new agent.
- Scoping a `permission` value and justifying every `allow`.
- Deciding whether a `tools:` list still belongs in the file.

**Core Principle**: Default to the least authority that still lets the role do its job, then justify every `allow` against the role description.

17: # Integration and Lifecycle: Wiring, Revising and Retiring a Rule
18: 
19: A rule file that nothing points at is inert.
20: 
21: ---
22: 
23: ## 1. OVERVIEW
24: 
25: The router's trigger table is the only thing that **loads** one; the pointer from the
26: governed `AGENTS.md` section is the only thing that makes it **findable at the moment
27: of need**.
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## 2. THE THREE WIRING POINTS
32: 
33: | Point | Where | Lost without it |
34: |-------|-------|-----------------|
35: | **Trigger row** | `REPO RULES.md` §2 | The rule never loads. Nothing else in the system fires a rule file |
36: | **Index row** | `REPO RULES.md` §3 | The rule is unbrowsable — reachable only by already knowing its trigger |
37: | **Governed-section pointer** | The `AGENTS.md` section it expands | The rule is discoverable at session start and invisible at the moment of need. This is the one people skip |
38: 
39: **Required:** every shipped rule has its trigger row and its index row, and
40: `check-repo-rules.cjs` fails the corpus when either is missing. The governed-section
41: pointer is the default, not a gate: a rule that expands an `AGENTS.md` section gets a
42: pointer there, and a rule governing two areas gets one in each. A rule whose subject no
43: `AGENTS.md` section states is reached through its trigger row alone. Count the live
44: pointers with `grep -c <rule-file> AGENTS.md` rather than trusting a number written here.
45: 
46: ---
=== 56-70
56:   **Out**. The router would have routed to a rule it declared out of bounds.
57: - Moving communication down while §4 said nothing about how a reply reads.
58: 
59: All four were caught and the boundary was widened deliberately each time, the third
60: being the narrow routing carve-out that admits verifying wiring you changed while still
61: refusing route selection. **A fifth widening that admitted selection itself would
62: dissolve the boundary the set exists to hold** — if the scope statement excludes a
63: proposal, that is a refusal, not a paperwork problem. The mode does not widen §4
64: unilaterally; that is an operator decision, and each of the four was one.
65: 
66: ---
67: 
68: ## 4. CREATE
69: 
70: Order matters, and it is chosen so an interruption is survivable.
71: 
72: 1. **Scope check** (§3 above). Refuse here if it fails.
73: 2. **Write the rule file.** First, deliberately.
74: 3. **Add the trigger row.**
75: 4. **Add the index row.**
76: 5. **Add the pointer** to each `AGENTS.md` section the rule governs.
77: 6. **Verify**: every link resolves; trigger rows, index rows and rule files are all the
78:    same count.

# Changelog & Release Notes Templates - Format Reference

Two narrative formats for global component changelogs and their GitHub release notes. Every rule below serves one goal: the reader learns what changed for them and why, in the fewest words that still carry the connection.

## 1. OVERVIEW

### The Canonical Exemplar

`.skilled/changelog/skilled/v4.0.0.0.md` is the house style, so read it before writing. It shows the opening narrative, Why This Release, What's New at a Glance, topical H2 sections with benefit-led H4 items, inline Breaking markers and Upgrade Notes. Copy its voice and shape, not its length: it records a major release, and most releases need a fraction of it. Older entries in the same folders predate this style, so do not copy them. When this template and the exemplar disagree on shape, the exemplar wins and the discrepancy is recorded.

### Usage

The `/create:changelog` workflow reads this template at step 4. Section 5 picks the format. Packet-local changelogs are deprecated and no longer written (section 7).

---

## 2. THE TWO TIERS

Every entry opens with the frontmatter block that SKILL.md section 5 defines. An editorial title H1 may follow it, and then the prose starts with the summary narrative. The retired machine header (a bare version title, a backlink, a version-date line) stays gone.

### Compact Format (under 10 changes, non-breaking)

---
title: "{component} v{VERSION}"
description: "{What the release changed, in one or two plain sentences of 250 characters at most.}"
